These microbes help digest food, especially fibre, make some vitamins such as vitamin K, train the immune system and crowd out harmful germs. A baby first receives microbes at birth and from breast milk, and the microbiome develops through childhood and is shaped by diet, environment and medicines.

Imbalances have been linked to conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, allergies and obesity. Antibiotics can disturb it. Fermented foods, such as yoghurt and the Azerbaijani qatiq, contain live bacteria, and a diet rich in fibre supports a healthy gut. Doctors can even treat some serious gut infections with faecal transplants.

articles.title: Hippocrates
articles.description: The ancient Greek father of medicine.
articles.content:
Hippocrates (about 460–370 BCE) was a Greek physician from the island of Kos, often called the father of medicine. He and his followers helped separate medicine from superstition by insisting that diseases have natural causes and should be treated based on careful observation.

The Hippocratic Corpus, a collection of about 60 works written by him and his school, describes symptoms, diagnosis and treatments, and emphasises diet, rest and the healing power of nature. It supported the theory of the four humours, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, which dominated medicine for about two thousand years, though it was wrong.

The Hippocratic Oath, a code of medical ethics traditionally attributed to him, requires doctors to help patients and keep their confidences. Versions of it are still used at some medical school graduations.

articles.title: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
articles.description: The medieval physician whose Canon guided doctors for centuries.
articles.content:
Avicenna, or Ibn Sina (980–1037), was a Persian scholar born near Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan, who became one of the most influential physicians and philosophers in history. He wrote in Arabic and worked in cities of Central Asia and Persia, and died in Hamadan.

His masterpiece, The Canon of Medicine, completed around 1025, is a huge encyclopaedia that gathered Greek, Roman, Persian and Indian medical knowledge and added his own observations. It described the contagious nature of some diseases, the importance of quarantine and the principles of testing medicines. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, it was a standard textbook in European universities until the 17th century.

He also wrote The Book of Healing, a wide-ranging work on philosophy and science. He is honoured across Asia, and a statue of him stands in the United Nations building in Vienna.

articles.title: Louis Pasteur
articles.description: The scientist who proved germs cause disease.
articles.content:
Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) was a French chemist and microbiologist whose discoveries changed medicine and industry. He showed that microbes cause fermentation and that spontaneous generation, the idea that life arises from non-living matter, is false, through experiments with flasks with long curved necks.

His work supported the germ theory of disease, the idea that specific microbes cause specific illnesses. He developed pasteurisation, heating liquids such as milk, wine and beer to kill harmful microbes, in the 1860s, which made food safer.

Pasteur also created vaccines. In 1881 he publicly demonstrated a vaccine against anthrax in sheep, and in 1885 he gave the first rabies vaccine to a boy, Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog and survived. The Pasteur Institute in Paris, founded in 1887, continues his work.

articles.title: Alexander Fleming
articles.description: The discoverer of penicillin.
articles.content:
Alexander Fleming (1881–1955) was a Scottish physician and microbiologist who discovered penicillin, the first true antibiotic. He served as a doctor in World War I, where he saw many soldiers die from infected wounds, which influenced his research.

In September 1928, at St Mary's Hospital in London, he returned from holiday to find that a mould, later identified as Penicillium, had contaminated a dish of Staphylococcus bacteria, and around the mould the bacteria had been killed. He realised that the mould released a substance that fights bacteria, and named it penicillin. He had earlier discovered lysozyme, a natural antibacterial enzyme, in 1921.

Fleming did not develop it into a medicine. That was done by Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their team in Oxford in the 1940s, and the three shared the Nobel Prize in 1945. In his acceptance speech Fleming warned that misuse could cause bacteria to become resistant.

articles.title: Andreas Vesalius
articles.description: The founder of modern human anatomy.
articles.content:
Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) was a Flemish physician who is regarded as the founder of modern human anatomy. He studied in Leuven, Paris and Padua, and became a professor in Padua, Italy, at the age of 23.

For centuries doctors had relied on the writings of the ancient Roman physician Galen, who had mostly dissected animals. Vesalius insisted on dissecting human bodies himself and found more than 200 errors in Galen's work. In 1543, the same year that Copernicus published his book on the Sun-centred universe, he published De humani corporis fabrica, The Fabric of the Human Body.

The book, with beautiful illustrations by artists from Titian's workshop, was one of the most influential works in medical history, and it showed that direct observation is the basis of medicine.

articles.title: Fingerprints
articles.description: The unique patterns on our fingertips.
articles.content:
A fingerprint is the pattern of ridges and valleys on the skin of a fingertip. These patterns form in the womb, between about the 10th and 16th weeks of pregnancy, and stay the same throughout life, apart from growth. Even identical twins have different fingerprints.

There are three main patterns: loops, which are the most common, whorls and arches. The ridges probably improve grip and increase sensitivity to touch. Sweat pores along the ridges leave prints on the objects we touch.

The British scientist Francis Galton showed in his 1892 book that fingerprints are permanent and unique. That year in Argentina, police official Juan Vucetich used a fingerprint to solve a murder, considered the first case of its kind. Fingerprints are now used in police work, passports, and to unlock phones.

articles.title: Twins
articles.description: Two babies born from the same pregnancy.
articles.content:
Twins are two offspring produced in the same pregnancy. About one in every 40 births in the world results in twins, though the rate varies by region and has increased with fertility treatments.

Identical twins, or monozygotic twins, develop from one fertilised egg that splits in two, so they share nearly all their DNA and are always the same sex. Fraternal twins, or dizygotic twins, develop from two separate eggs fertilised by two sperm, and are as genetically similar as ordinary siblings, and can be of different sexes.

Scientists study twins to find out how much of our traits come from genes and how much from the environment. Identical twins are very similar in many ways but are not exactly the same, and they have different fingerprints. Rarely, twins are born joined together, called conjoined twins.

articles.title: Left- and Right-Handedness
articles.description: Why most people prefer one hand.
articles.content:
Handedness is the tendency to use one hand more skilfully than the other. About 90% of people are right-handed and about 10% are left-handed, and a small number can use both hands equally well, called ambidextrous.

Handedness is linked to the way the brain is organised: each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. In most people, the left hemisphere handles language and controls the right hand. Genes have some effect, but it is not simple, and left-handed parents can have right-handed children. Hand preference can be seen in the womb, and babies show it in the first years.

In the past left-handed children were often forced to write with their right hands, and the word sinister comes from the Latin for left. Today it is accepted as normal. International Left-Handers Day is observed on 13 August.

articles.title: Yawning
articles.description: The contagious mystery of the open mouth.
articles.content:
A yawn is an involuntary act of opening the mouth wide and taking a deep breath, followed by a slower exhale. It typically lasts about four to seven seconds. Yawning is found across most vertebrates, including fish, birds, dogs and apes, and human babies yawn in the womb from about 11 weeks.

Scientists are still not sure why we yawn. The old idea that it increases oxygen has been disproved. Current hypotheses include that yawning cools the brain, helps us become more alert when we are tired or bored, and helps in shifting between different states of wakefulness.

Yawning is contagious: seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can make us yawn too. This effect begins at about age four or five in children and may be related to empathy and social bonding, though this is debated.

articles.title: Laughter
articles.description: The social sound of joy.
articles.content:
Laughter is a response to humour, joy or social situations, involving a series of short, repetitive sounds and movements of the face and chest. It uses about 15 facial muscles and briefly changes breathing. Babies begin to laugh at around three to four months old, before they can speak.

Laughter is deeply social: we are much more likely to laugh with other people than alone, and it is contagious. It signals friendliness, eases tension and strengthens bonds. It also releases endorphins and reduces levels of the stress hormone cortisol, and it temporarily raises our tolerance for pain.

Laughter is not unique to humans. Chimpanzees and other apes make laughter-like sounds when tickled or playing, and researchers have found that rats emit high-pitched chirps when tickled, which humans cannot hear. Laughter appears to be a very old form of play communication.

articles.title: Human Height
articles.description: How tall we grow and why.
articles.content:
Human height varies widely between individuals and populations. The average adult man is about 171 centimetres tall around the world, and the average adult woman about 159 centimetres. People in the Netherlands and some other European countries are among the tallest, with average male heights of about 183 centimetres.

Height is largely inherited, with genes accounting for about 80% of the difference between people, but nutrition and health in childhood also matter. Children grow fastest in infancy and during the growth spurt of puberty. Growth continues as long as the growth plates at the ends of long bones remain open, and they close at the end of adolescence.

The tallest person in recorded history was Robert Wadlow of the United States, who reached 272 centimetres, and the shortest adult recorded was Chandra Bahadur Dangi of Nepal, at 54.6 centimetres. People are about a centimetre taller in the morning than in the evening, because the discs in the spine compress during the day.
